title: Scaling writes: batching
seriesDescription: How to scale write-heavy systems in an interview: vertical scaling and database choice, sharding and partition keys, vertical partitioning, queues and load shedding, batching, hierarchical aggregation, and the resharding and hot-key deep dives.
description: Amortising per-write overhead at the application, in an intermediate process, or in the database, and when batching helps or backfires.
source: Study notes: the scaling writes pattern

questions.prompt: Why does batching writes improve throughput?

options.text: It amortises network round trips, transaction setup and index overhead across many writes.
options.why: Right: fixed costs are paid once.

options.text: It removes the need for the database to store data.
options.why: The data is still stored.

options.text: It makes every write instantaneous under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Latency can go up; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: It guarantees no data is ever lost as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: It can raise the risk of loss.

questions.explanation: Databases usually handle batches more efficiently than individual writes.

questions.prompt: A service reads from a Kafka topic, processes, then writes to a database. Why is batching in the application safe here?

options.text: If it crashes it can re-read the topic, so nothing is lost.
options.why: Right: Kafka is the durable source.

options.text: Kafka deletes messages as soon as they are read.
options.why: It retains them; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Databases cannot accept batches from Kafka consumers.
options.why: They can; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: The application is the only copy of the data.
options.why: That is the unsafe case.

questions.explanation: When the app is the source of truth, a crash can lose confirmed writes held in a batch.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of batching writes in an app that is the source of truth?

options.text: A crash after confirming requests but before committing the batch loses those writes.
options.why: Right: acknowledged data vanishes.

options.text: Batches are always rejected by the database under normal operating conditions.
options.why: They are accepted; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Batching makes writes slower for every client in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads.
options.why: It usually speeds the database.

options.text: There is no risk if batches are small.
options.why: Any batch has some exposure.

questions.explanation: Not all applications can tolerate that.

questions.prompt: A Like Batcher reads like events, counts per post per minute, and writes the totals. What does it achieve?

options.text: 100 likes on a post in a minute become one write.
options.why: Right: far fewer database operations.

options.text: It stops users from liking posts twice in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Deduplication is another concern.

options.text: It moves the likes to the user's device as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: It stays server-side; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: It makes every like visible instantly.
options.why: Visibility is delayed by the window.

questions.explanation: It adds a little latency and another moving part.

questions.prompt: Most posts get one like an hour. Does a one-minute batching window help?

options.text: No: with so few events per window, there is almost nothing to combine.
options.why: Right: check batching efficacy.

options.text: Yes, always, because smaller windows are better without any extra configuration.
options.why: It only helps if events collide.

options.text: Yes, because it cuts the number of posts.
options.why: It does not change post count.

options.text: Only if the window is shorter than a second in a typical production setup.
options.why: A shorter window helps even less.

questions.explanation: Staff-level answers consider whether batching actually reduces writes.

questions.prompt: How does flushing every 100 ms instead of every write help a store like Redis?

options.text: Many writes share one disk flush, since disk is the usual bottleneck.
options.why: Right: the big hammer, for extreme cases.

options.text: It stores each write twice for safety for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: It reduces flushes, not duplicates.

options.text: It removes the need for memory.
options.why: Data still lives in memory.

options.text: It makes data durable instantly as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: It widens the window of possible loss.

questions.explanation: Reserve database-level batching for extreme cases.

questions.prompt: True or false: batching trades a little latency and extra moving parts for far fewer, cheaper writes.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: that is the trade.

options.text: False
options.why: It does cost some latency and complexity.

questions.explanation: It is a trade-off, and you should name both sides.
